title: AUGUST 11 DEADLINE DAY! McBride & Towns Extension HOUR ZERO + Center Search STALLS!
thumb_prompt: A dramatic countdown clock showing 11:59 PM mounted on the Madison Square Garden jumbotron, with unsigned contract papers scattered on a desk below, casting shadows under harsh deadline lighting, while an hourglass with orange and blue sand runs empty in the foreground.
thumb_subject: a determined guard in a blue and orange number two jersey standing at a crossroads with his arms crossed

paragraphs.text: Welcome to Knicks Daily. Today is August eleventh, twenty twenty six. And if you know your CBA rules, you know exactly what that means. This is the deadline. Not for signing extensions, no. This is far more subtle and far more important. This is the last day the Knicks can extend Deuce McBride or Karl Anthony Towns and still maintain the ability to trade them before February's deadline. Six months from today is February eleventh, twenty twenty seven, the trade deadline. Any veteran extension signed after midnight tonight locks that player in place until mid-season. For a front office navigating the second apron, for a team with championship aspirations and brutal financial constraints, this date matters. And as the sun sets on August eleventh, neither Deuce nor Karl have signed anything.

Now let's be clear about what this does and doesn't mean. This deadline expiring doesn't prevent the Knicks from extending either player tomorrow or next week or in October. They absolutely can still get deals done. What it does is send a signal. If the Knicks were planning to extend Deuce and wanted to preserve maximum roster flexibility, including the theoretical ability to flip him in a midseason deal if some blockbuster opportunity emerged, they needed to do it by today. The fact that they're letting this deadline pass tells you something about their intentions. It might tell you they're keeping him and don't need trade flexibility. Or it might tell you they're already considering moving him and don't want to complicate that by adding a new contract into the equation.

This is the exact same situation that played out with Mikal Bridges last summer. The Knicks extended Bridges just under the six month cutoff, which kept him tradeable for the Giannis Antetokounmpo sweepstakes that was rumored all season. They didn't move Bridges, thank goodness, but maintaining that option was strategic. Leon Rose's front office thinks in chess moves, not checkers. Every decision preserves future flexibility. Every contract signed considers not just today's roster but next February's trade market and next summer's cap sheet. That's how championship teams operate above the second apron. You cannot afford to box yourself in. One wrong move and you're locked into a roster you can't improve.

Let's start with Deuce McBride because his situation is simpler and more urgent. Miles McBride is eligible for a four year extension worth up to ninety five million dollars. He's making just under four million next season, an absolute bargain for a guard who ranked in the ninety third percentile of defensive matchup difficulty and the ninety ninth percentile of three point shot making. He's an elite three and D player on a dirt cheap contract. The Knicks were five point four points better per one hundred possessions with him on the floor over the past two seasons. He's also an NBA champion who closed out playoff games. On paper, extending him is a no brainer. But the Knicks are letting today pass without a deal. Why?

The answer is guard depth and future cost. The Knicks already have Jalen Brunson locked in long term. They have Jose Alvarado signed through twenty twenty eight on a team friendly deal. They have Landry Shamet. They drafted and stashed Tyler Nickel, who is reportedly leaning toward signing with the team rather than returning to college. New York's backcourt is crowded. And while Deuce is excellent, he's not irreplaceable. If he wants something close to that ninety five million dollar max, the Knicks might decide they can find similar production for less money. Or they can trade him now, while he's on that cheap expiring contract, and get assets back before he walks for nothing in free agency next summer.
card_lines: Trade now or lose him for nothing?

paragraphs.text: Here's the pattern under Leon Rose that tells you what's coming. The Knicks don't move key players until they're entering contract years. Julius Randle got traded the offseason before his player option. Immanuel Quickley got shipped to Toronto months before restricted free agency. Donte DiVincenzo only got moved because Karl Anthony Towns fell into their lap. McBride has one more year on his contract, which means the pressure isn't on yet. The Knicks can wait. They can let him play out this season on that cheap deal, see if anyone in the young guard group emerges, and then make a decision next summer. If they trade him now, it's because an offer they can't refuse came in. Otherwise, expect Deuce to still be in a Knicks uniform when training camp opens in October.
card_lines: McBride has 1 year left = safe for now

paragraphs.text: But the August eleventh deadline passing does lower his trade value. Right now Deuce is appealing because he's cheap and under contract. If the Knicks extend him to something reasonable, say four years and sixty million, that makes him even more attractive to trade partners because you're getting organizational control without the threat of free agency. But if they don't extend him, teams trading for McBride know they're getting an expiring contract who could walk next summer. That uncertainty lowers what they'll give up. It's the classic trade value paradox. You want to extend a guy to boost his value, but extending him costs you flexibility. So you gamble that his on court impact this season is worth more than whatever you'd get back in a trade. It's a high stakes calculation that NBA front offices make every day.

sections.heading: Karl Anthony Towns: The Two Hundred Seventy Two Million Dollar Question

paragraphs.text: Now we get to the big one. Karl Anthony Towns. The man who delivered the Knicks their first championship in fifty three years. The guy who averaged over twenty five points and eleven rebounds in the Finals against Victor Wembanyama. The center who was, at worst, the third most important player on a title team. He's eligible for a four year, two hundred seventy two million dollar extension. That's max money. That's franchise altering money. And according to every report out there, the Knicks are not offering it. James Edwards of The Athletic wrote that he's certain the Knicks will offer Towns an extension, but he doesn't expect it to be the full max. The Knicks want to leave room in their wallet to maintain financial flexibility. And just like with McBride, they're letting August eleventh pass without a deal.

Here's why that two hundred seventy two million dollar number is so terrifying for James Dolan and Leon Rose. If Towns signs that full max, the Knicks project to sit roughly thirteen million dollars below the second apron next season while still needing to fill several roster spots. That's cutting it incredibly close. And it gets worse in future years. Jalen Brunson becomes eligible for a new max contract in twenty twenty eight. OG Anunoby will be due another extension. Josh Hart needs to get paid. If you give Towns the full max now, you're essentially locking yourself into the second apron for the next four years. You lose your ability to aggregate salaries in trades. You can't take back more money than you send out. Your roster building tools evaporate. That's why the Knicks are hesitating.
card_lines: Still need to fill roster spots
Locks team into apron for 4 years

paragraphs.text: There's also the Jalen Brunson precedent hanging over this entire negotiation. Brunson took a stunning discount last summer, leaving one hundred thirteen million dollars on the table by signing a one hundred fifty six point five million dollar extension instead of waiting for his full max. He did it to give the team flexibility. He did it to help them build a championship roster. And it worked. They won the title. Now there's an expectation, fair or not, that Towns should do the same thing. Some people expect that Karl Anthony Towns is going to have to sacrifice the same way Brunson did. But here's the thing. Towns already sacrificed once. He was eligible for a max extension last offseason and the Knicks didn't offer him anything. He stayed focused and delivered a championship. Should he really be expected to take another discount after proving his worth?

The strategic element here is fascinating. Towns absolutely knows about this August eleventh deadline. He knows that signing before today makes him tradeable in season. He knows that waiting until after today protects him from being moved before February. So if you're Towns and you're negotiating with a team that won't offer you the full max, why would you ever sign before this deadline? Even if you trust the Knicks to keep you, even if you love New York and want to stay, you wait until midnight tonight. You strip every iota of uncertainty from the equation. You protect yourself. That's smart business. And that's exactly what's happening. The deadline will pass. Towns won't sign today. And starting tomorrow, the real negotiations begin.

Here's what I think happens. The Knicks offer Towns something between two hundred and two hundred thirty million over four years. Not the full max, but close enough to be respectful. Towns counters at two fifty. They settle somewhere around two hundred twenty million, which saves the Knicks fifty million in cap space and flexibility over the life of the deal. Towns gets his money, the Knicks get their flexibility, and both sides win. The alternative is that Towns decides he's done taking discounts, holds firm at the max, and the Knicks let him play out his contract. He has a player option for sixty one million in twenty twenty seven. He could opt in, opt out, test free agency. That uncertainty would hang over the franchise all season. I don't think it comes to that. But August eleventh passing without a deal means we're heading into the season without clarity on the most important contract question the Knicks face.

Speaking of extension eligible players, Josh Hart technically became eligible for a four year extension yesterday, on August tenth. Hart could sign for over thirty million per year, up to roughly one hundred thirty one million total. But unlike McBride and Towns, there's zero urgency with Hart because the Knicks control his future. He has a twenty two million dollar team option for twenty twenty seven twenty eight. New York holds all the leverage. They can extend him whenever they want. They can wait until next summer. They can exercise the option and then extend him. Hart isn't going anywhere. And according to multiple reports, Hart is expected to take a team friendly deal to help the Knicks navigate the second apron, just like Brunson did. Hart has said publicly he doesn't want to play deep into his thirties. He turns thirty two next March. This might be his last contract. But he's also a champion now, a key part of the Knicks identity, and he clearly values winning over maximizing every dollar.

The smart move for the Knicks is to wait on Hart until they settle the Towns situation. Towns is the flight risk. Towns is the guy who could opt out and leave. Hart is under team control. So you prioritize the Towns negotiation, figure out what that deal looks like, see how much cap space you have left, and then you circle back to Hart with an offer that fits your remaining flexibility. Spotrac reported just hours ago that getting Hart inked is less likely than Towns because the Knicks can afford to wait. And from a roster construction standpoint, that's the right call. You build from your biggest question mark down to your most secure pieces. Hart is secure. So Hart waits. And I'd bet we don't hear about a Hart extension until after Labor Day at the earliest, and possibly not until the season starts.
card_lines: Hart likely waits until Labor Day

paragraphs.text: While the extension drama plays out, the Knicks still have a roster hole that's getting more glaring by the day. They need a third center behind Karl Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond. They lost Mitchell Robinson to the Celtics in free agency. Ariel Hukporti went to the Sixers. The Knicks currently have just thirteen players on standard contracts and all three two way slots remain open. They've spent all summer hunting for a big man and have come up empty. According to Ian Begley of SNY, the Knicks have contacted several free agent centers in recent weeks, but no signing appears imminent. If they were prepared to give a guaranteed deal to any of those players, it would have happened by now. The fact that it hasn't tells you the Knicks either don't love the options or they're holding out hope for a trade.

The Knicks have been aggressive in their pursuit. They tried to trade for Yves Missi from the Pelicans and got rejected multiple times. They put an offer sheet on Dallas restricted free agent Moussa Cisse, two years and four point seven million, but Dallas matched it. They're reportedly monitoring Moussa Diabate from the Hornets, a young rim runner with upside. Charlotte also has Ryan Kalkbrenner behind Diabate, another intriguing young big. But none of these trades have materialized. And on the free agent market, the pickings are slim. Nick Richards is probably the best option still available. He averaged nine point four points and seven point six rebounds after being traded to the Bulls last season. He's athletic, he's a lob threat, he can protect the rim. But does he want to sign a minimum deal to be the third string center on a championship team? That's the question.

Here's the problem the Knicks face. They have three point three million dollars of space below the second apron. They have minimum contracts to offer. They cannot take back more salary than they send out in a trade without going over the apron. Those constraints make it incredibly hard to add impact players. If you're a free agent center, you can probably get more money and a bigger role somewhere else. If you're a team with a young center the Knicks want, you're asking for Deuce McBride or Tyler Kolek in return, and the Knicks don't want to part with those guys for a backup big. It's a standoff. And August is traditionally the quietest month on the NBA calendar. The longer this drags on without a resolution, the more likely it becomes that the Knicks enter training camp with just Towns and Drummond at the five.
card_lines: Can't take back more in trades

paragraphs.text: The next checkpoint is training camp roster construction. If the Knicks enter September without adding a credible third center, this becomes a real storyline heading into the season. What happens if Towns or Drummond gets hurt? What happens in foul trouble? The Knicks won a championship last season in part because Karl Anthony Towns stayed healthy all playoffs. But you cannot count on that repeating. Depth matters over an eighty two game season. The Knicks know this. Leon Rose knows this. But sometimes you can't force a deal that isn't there. Sometimes you have to accept that the market dried up, the options disappeared, and you're going to have to make do with what you have. That might be where we're headed. And if it is, the Knicks will pivot to small ball lineups with Josh Hart or OG Anunoby playing small ball five in emergency situations. It's not ideal. But championship teams adapt.
card_lines: What if Towns or Drummond hurt?
Can't force deals that aren't there

sections.heading: Rookie Decisions: Jack Kayil and Tyler Nickel

paragraphs.text: While we're talking about roster construction, let's touch on the two second round picks from the twenty twenty six draft. Jack Kayil, the thirty ninth pick, announced last week that he's spending the season with Alba Berlin rather than joining the Knicks immediately. This was always the most likely outcome. Kayil is a twenty year old guard who wanted to come straight to the NBA, but the Knicks' second apron constraints made signing him basically impossible. So he goes to Europe, gets significant developmental minutes with a top tier club, and the Knicks retain his NBA rights. It's a clean draft and stash move. In two or three years, when the Knicks have more roster flexibility, Kayil can come over and compete for a rotation spot. Until then, he develops overseas. It's a win win. The Knicks get a free asset developing on someone else's dime. Kayil gets playing time instead of riding the bench in Westchester.
card_lines: Wanted NBA but no roster space

paragraphs.text: Tyler Nickel, the forty seventh pick, is the more interesting case. According to multiple reports, Nickel is leaning toward signing with the Knicks rather than returning to college. He was recently granted a fifth year of NCAA eligibility in a federal court ruling, though the NCAA is appealing. So Nickel has options. He could go back to school, develop another year, potentially improve his draft stock. Or he could sign with New York, either on a standard deal or a two way contract, and start his professional career now. Hoops Rumors reported just hours ago that Nickel is leaning toward going pro. If he signs, he gives the Knicks another young guard with shooting upside. Nickel was everything the Knicks could want at Summer League. He backed up his reputation as one of the draft's top shooters. That skill translates immediately. The question is whether the Knicks have roster space for him. They have three two way slots open. Nickel on a two way makes a lot of sense.

sections.heading: Historical Context: Extension Deadlines That Changed Everything

paragraphs.text: Extension deadlines have shaped Knicks history more than people realize. Let's go back to August twenty eighth, twenty twenty two. The Knicks were deep in talks with the Jazz about trading for Donovan Mitchell. RJ Barrett was the centerpiece going back. But Leon Rose gave Utah a Monday deadline. Make the trade or we're extending Barrett. Utah didn't bite. The Knicks extended Barrett to four years and one hundred twenty million. That extension made Barrett virtually untradeable for months because of poison pill provisions. It effectively ended the Mitchell sweepstakes. Utah traded Mitchell to Cleveland instead. At the time, Knicks fans were furious. They wanted the star. But here's the twist. That Barrett extension gave the Knicks the salary they needed two years later to trade for Karl Anthony Towns. Barrett went to Minnesota in that deal. If the Knicks had traded him for Mitchell in twenty twenty two, they never get Towns. And without Towns, do they win the title? Probably not.
card_lines: Made Barrett untradeable, ended Mitchell pursuit

paragraphs.text: Extension timing is everything in the modern NBA. The poison pill provision means that a player on a rookie extension counts as different salary amounts for the trading team versus the acquiring team. It's a deliberate CBA feature designed to discourage teams from flipping first round picks immediately after extending them. But it creates this strategic chess game. If you extend a guy too early, you limit your trade options. If you wait too long, you risk him getting to restricted free agency where another team can make your life miserable with an offer sheet. The Knicks have learned this lesson repeatedly. Immanuel Quickley never got extended. They let him get to restricted free agency, then traded him to Toronto in the OG Anunoby deal before anyone could offer sheet him. Mitchell Robinson never got extended either. They let him hit free agency and he walked to Boston. Sometimes you extend. Sometimes you trade. Sometimes you let them walk. It all depends on value, fit, and timing.

The most painful extension deadline in recent Knicks memory might be Kristaps Porzingis in twenty eighteen. The Knicks could have extended Porzingis that summer before his fourth season. He was coming off an All Star year, averaging twenty two points and six boards. The Knicks balked at offering the full max because of injury concerns. Porzingis had already torn his ACL in February. The relationship soured. By January twenty nineteen, the Knicks traded him to Dallas in a salary dump to clear cap space for the twenty nineteen free agency class. They were chasing Kevin Durant and Kyrie Irving. They got neither. Dallas got Porzingis. The Knicks got cap space they wasted on Julius Randle, Bobby Portis, and Taj Gibson. It was a disaster. The lesson? Sometimes you pay the guy. Sometimes the injury risk is worth it if the alternative is losing the asset for nothing. The Knicks learned that lesson the hard way. And it's informed every extension decision they've made since Leon Rose took over.
card_lines: Balked at max due to ACL injury

paragraphs.text: So here's where we stand as the sun sets on August eleventh, twenty twenty six. Deuce McBride will not be extended before midnight. The Knicks are keeping their options open. They'll let him play out the season on his cheap deal and reassess next summer. If a trade offer comes in during the season that blows them away, they can still pull the trigger. Karl Anthony Towns will not be extended before midnight. The real negotiations start tomorrow. Expect something to get done before training camp, probably in the two hundred to two hundred thirty million dollar range. Josh Hart will wait until the Towns situation resolves. The Knicks will circle back to him in September or October with a team friendly offer that he'll probably accept. The center search continues. Don't expect a signing until September at the earliest. The Knicks might go into camp with just Towns and Drummond. And the rookies will sort themselves out over the next few weeks.

This is the life of a championship team navigating the second apron. You cannot make impulsive decisions. You cannot overpay just to get deals done. You have to be patient, strategic, and willing to let deadlines pass if the right deal isn't there. Leon Rose has proven over and over that he understands this. He waited on Brunson and got him for a discount. He waited on OG Anunoby and got him extended. He'll wait on Towns and McBride and Hart until the numbers make sense. And if the numbers never make sense, he'll pivot. That's what elite front offices do. They don't panic. They don't overpay. They build championship rosters one smart decision at a time. The Knicks won their first title in fifty three years with that approach. They'll defend it with the same approach. August eleventh was just another checkpoint on that journey. The deadline passed. Life goes on. And the Knicks keep building.
card_lines: Rose's track record: wait for value
Won title this way, defend it this way

paragraphs.text: That's it for today's episode of Knicks Daily. Tomorrow we'll know more. Tomorrow the Towns talks heat up without the deadline hanging over them. Tomorrow we see if any center news breaks. But today, August eleventh, was about what didn't happen. No extensions. No signings. Just the sound of a deadline passing and a front office staying patient. In today's NBA, sometimes the best move is the one you don't make. Sometimes the smartest decision is to wait one more day. The Knicks waited. And starting tomorrow, we'll see if that patience pays off. Thanks for watching. Hit subscribe if you haven't already. Drop a comment with your prediction on where the Towns extension lands. And I'll see you tomorrow with whatever news breaks overnight. Until then, let's go Knicks.
card_lines: Best move = the one you don't make
